title: Seven Days
excerpt: Maya receives a message predicting her death in exactly seven days. The first detail comes true before sunrise.
content:
Day One — Monday, 12:01 a.m.

Maya Cole woke to the sound of her phone vibrating beneath her pillow.

At first, she ignored it.

Rain tapped against the bedroom window, and the air conditioner hummed softly above her head. Somewhere outside, a motorcycle passed through the wet street, its engine fading into the distance.

She had been dreaming about her mother again.

In the dream, her mother stood at the end of a long corridor, wearing the pale-blue dress she had worn on the day she disappeared. Her face was hidden by darkness, but Maya could hear her voice.

When the seventh day comes, don't open the door.

Then the phone vibrated again.

Maya reached beneath the pillow and pulled it out.

12:01 a.m.

Unknown number.

She almost dismissed the notification. Spam messages had become a regular nuisance, especially since she had published her recent investigation into a series of unexplained deaths in Lagos.

But the message contained only nine words.

You have seven days left to live, Maya.

She stared at the screen.

Then she laughed.

It was a short, uncomfortable laugh, the kind people made when something frightened them but they refused to admit it.

“Very funny,” she muttered.

She took a screenshot and typed a reply.

Who is this?

The message showed as delivered.

No response came.

Maya tossed the phone onto the bedside table and lay back down.

She was twenty-nine years old, an investigative journalist, and the sort of person who believed that almost every mystery had a reasonable explanation. Someone had found her number. Someone wanted attention. Perhaps it was a disgruntled reader who disliked her latest article.

She had received threats before.

Three months earlier, a businessman she had exposed for embezzling charitable donations had sent her a message warning her to stop digging. Another man had waited outside her office for two hours before security escorted him away.

Neither incident had frightened her enough to stop working.

This message would be no different.

She switched off the bedside lamp.

Her phone vibrated again.

Maya closed her eyes.

It vibrated a third time.

With an irritated sigh, she picked it up.

A second message had arrived.

Tomorrow, at 8:17 a.m., you will hear a gunshot. Do not turn around.

Maya sat up.

The bedroom suddenly seemed smaller.

She read the message again, then checked the number.

It was a Nigerian mobile number, but searching her contacts produced nothing.

She called it.

The call connected immediately.

For three seconds, she heard nothing but faint static.

Then a man whispered, “You should have stayed out of the Meridian case.”

Maya's blood went cold.

The Meridian case.

She hadn't written about it publicly.

Six months earlier, she had begun investigating Meridian House, a private medical facility that had closed unexpectedly after several patients disappeared from its records. The facility had been owned by a charitable foundation with connections to wealthy businessmen, politicians, and senior medical professionals.

Her editor had killed the investigation after receiving a letter from the foundation's lawyers.

Maya had continued working on it privately.

Only four people knew she had kept the files.

Her editor, Daniel.

Her best friend, Tessa.

A retired police officer who had helped her obtain old documents.

And Maya herself.

“Who are you?” she demanded.

The man breathed into the receiver.

“You don't remember me.”

“Tell me your name.”

A faint sound came through the phone.

It sounded like a woman crying.

Then the man said something that made Maya grip the phone so tightly that her fingers hurt.

“Your mother remembered me.”

The call ended.

Maya sat motionless in the darkness.

For eleven years, she had believed her mother, Evelyn Cole, had abandoned her family.

There had been no body, no confirmed sighting, and no explanation. One evening, Evelyn left home and never returned. The police searched for weeks before closing the missing-person investigation.

Maya had been sixteen.

Her father had refused to discuss it.

Two years later, he died in a road accident.

Since then, Maya had learned to live with unanswered questions.

But the man on the phone had known her mother's name.

And he had connected her disappearance to a case Maya had never published.

She switched on the lamp and spent the next hour searching the number online, checking old emails, and reviewing her notes on Meridian House.

Nothing.

At 2:13 a.m., she found something she had overlooked.

An old photograph.

It had been taken outside Meridian House in 2015, during the facility's official opening ceremony. The photograph showed a row of medical professionals standing beside the foundation's chairman, Victor Hale.

In the background, near a black vehicle, stood a woman in a pale-blue dress.

Maya zoomed in.

The woman looked like her mother.

She enlarged the image until the photograph became a blur of pixels.

The woman's face was partially turned away, but Maya recognized the shape of her jaw, the way she held her shoulders, and the small silver pendant she always wore.

Her mother had been at Meridian House.

One year before she disappeared.

Maya grabbed her laptop and began searching archived newspaper reports.

At 3:40 a.m., she found an article about a fire at the facility's research wing.

The fire had occurred eleven years earlier, on the exact date Evelyn vanished.

According to the report, the fire had destroyed several rooms and damaged medical records. No fatalities had been officially recorded.

But beneath the article was a comment from an anonymous reader.

The building didn't burn by accident.

Maya clicked the profile.

The account had been deleted.

She searched the sentence, hoping it had appeared elsewhere.

Nothing.

At 4:05 a.m., she finally slept.

And at 7:52 a.m., she woke to the sound of her alarm.

For a moment, the messages felt like a distant nightmare.

Then she remembered the prediction.

Tomorrow, at 8:17 a.m., you will hear a gunshot. Do not turn around.

She checked the time.

7:54.

Maya lived on the fourth floor of a residential building in Ikeja. Her apartment overlooked a narrow street lined with shops, parked cars, and small restaurants that opened early to serve commuters.

She showered, dressed, and made coffee.

At 8:03, she decided she was being ridiculous.

At 8:10, she left the apartment.

At 8:14, she reached the ground floor.

The security guard, an elderly man named Bako, was sitting beside the entrance, listening to a radio.

“Good morning, madam,” he said.

“Morning, Bako.”

“You look tired today.”

“I didn't sleep well.”

He nodded toward the road.

“Maybe you should take a taxi. The traffic is already bad.”

Maya smiled faintly.

“I'll walk to the junction.”

She stepped outside.

The morning was bright, with sunlight reflecting off the wet pavement. A woman was arranging vegetables at a roadside stall, and two schoolchildren argued beside a parked bus.

Everything seemed ordinary.

Maya checked her phone.

8:16 a.m.

She felt foolish for being nervous.

Then a black car sped around the corner.

Its tires struck a pothole, sending water splashing across the road. A man standing near a shop shouted angrily at the driver.

Maya stopped walking.

The car disappeared into traffic.

8:17 a.m.

A gunshot cracked through the street.

The sound was so sudden that several people screamed.

Maya froze.

A second shot followed.

Someone shouted, “Get down!”

People scattered.

Maya dropped behind a parked vehicle, her heart hammering against her ribs. She could hear footsteps, shouting, and the distant wail of a siren.

Then came silence.

She remained crouched for several seconds before slowly lifting her head.

Across the road, a man lay beside a motorcycle.

Blood spread beneath him.

A woman knelt nearby, screaming his name.

Maya recognized the victim.

It was Mr. Bako, the security guard from her building.

He had left his chair moments earlier to retrieve a package from a delivery rider.

Now he lay motionless on the pavement.

Maya's hands began to shake.

She looked at her phone.

8:18 a.m.

The prediction had been exact.

She hadn't been the one shot.

But she had heard the gunshot.

And Bako was dead.

Maya backed away from the scene, struggling to breathe. She wanted to call the police, but the phone felt slippery in her hand.

A new message appeared.

One down. Six days left.

She stared at it.

Then another message arrived.

You turned around.

Maya looked up sharply.

Across the street, a man in a grey suit stood beside a parked car.

He was watching her.

When their eyes met, he raised his phone and took a photograph.

Maya started toward him.

“Hey!”

He opened the car door.

“Stop!”

The engine roared to life.

The car pulled into traffic and vanished.

Maya tried to memorize the registration number, but she had seen only a few digits.

Her phone rang.

Daniel Okafor, her editor.

She answered immediately.

“Maya, where are you?”

“Something happened.”

“I know. I'm watching the news.”

“What do you mean?”

“There's been a shooting near your apartment. Someone sent footage to the newsroom.”

Maya looked toward the dead security guard.

“Who sent it?”

“I don't know. The video arrived anonymously.”

“Daniel, I need you to listen to me. Someone warned me this would happen.”

Silence.

“What did you say?”

“I received a message last night. It predicted the gunshot at exactly 8:17.”

Daniel exhaled slowly.

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

“Send me everything. The number, the messages, all of it.”

“I need you to help me investigate Meridian House.”

Another silence followed.

Longer this time.

“How do you know about Meridian House?” Maya asked.

Daniel's voice dropped.

“Maya, I thought you had stopped working on that story.”

“I never stopped.”

“You need to delete those files.”

“Why?”

“Because the people connected to that place aren't the sort of people you can expose in an article.”

“Someone just killed a man outside my home.”

“I know.”

“No, you don't understand. The person who sent the messages knew where I would be. They knew when the shooting would happen. They know about Meridian House, and they know about my mother.”

Daniel said nothing.

“Tell me what you know,” Maya demanded.

“I can't explain this over the phone.”

“Then meet me.”

“Not at the newsroom. Not at your apartment. I'll send you a location.”

The call ended.

Maya stood on the pavement as emergency responders arrived. She answered a few questions from the police, but she didn't mention the messages. Not yet.

She needed proof.

More importantly, she needed to know whether the killer had targeted Bako or whether the shooting had been intended for her.

By noon, she was sitting in a small café on a quiet street, reviewing the footage of the shooting on her laptop.

The video had been recorded from a shop across the road.

She watched the black car appear.

She watched the driver slow down near the junction.

Then she noticed something.

The driver's window had been open.

For a fraction of a second, a face appeared.

Maya paused the video.

She enlarged the image.

Her stomach tightened.

The driver was a woman.

A woman with dark hair and a small silver pendant around her neck.

Maya knew that pendant.

She had seen it in the photograph from Meridian House.

She had seen it in the last family photograph taken before her mother disappeared.

The woman driving the car looked exactly like Evelyn Cole.

Maya watched the footage again.

And again.

She knew it was possible that grief and fear were distorting her judgment. She knew that a blurry image could make strangers resemble people we desperately wanted to see.

But she couldn't ignore the evidence.

Her mother might be alive.

And if she was alive, she might have just killed a man.

At 3:26 p.m., Daniel sent the promised location.

An abandoned office building near the industrial district.

The message contained no explanation, only an address and a warning.

Come alone. Tell nobody.

Maya hesitated.

Then she remembered the unknown man's voice.

Your mother remembered me.

She packed her laptop, saved the footage to an encrypted drive, and left the café.

The office building stood behind a row of shuttered warehouses. Its windows were covered in dust, and weeds grew through cracks in the concrete.

Maya entered through an unlocked side door.

Inside, the air smelled of damp paper and rust.

“Daniel?” she called.

Her voice echoed through the empty corridor.

No answer.

She climbed the stairs to the second floor and found a door marked ROOM 204.

It was slightly open.

She pushed it.

The room contained a desk, two chairs, and a wall covered with photographs.

Photographs of missing people.

Photographs of crime scenes.

Photographs of buildings connected to Meridian House.

Maya stepped closer.

There were dozens of faces.

Some belonged to people she recognized from old news reports. Others were strangers.

In the center of the wall was a photograph of Evelyn Cole.

Beneath it, someone had written a date.

OCTOBER 29, 2015.

Tomorrow's date.

Maya heard the door close behind her.

She spun around.

Daniel stood in the doorway, his face pale.

“You came,” he said.

“What is all this?”

He didn't answer.

“Daniel, what happened at Meridian House?”

He walked toward the wall and removed a photograph.

It showed a young woman sitting in a hospital bed, her face bruised and her eyes fixed on the camera.

Maya recognized her.

It was her mother.

But the date on the photograph was from only three months ago.

“She's alive,” Maya whispered.

Daniel nodded.

“Your mother has been alive for eleven years.”

Maya felt as though the floor had tilted beneath her.

“Where is she?”

“I don't know.”

“You have a photograph from three months ago!”

“I received it anonymously.”

“Who sent it?”

Daniel looked at the floor.

“I think it was the same person who sent you the messages.”

Maya took a step toward him.

“Why didn't you tell me?”

“Because I was afraid.”

“Of what?”

He looked up.

“Of the seventh day.”

Before Maya could ask what he meant, the lights flickered.

A phone began ringing somewhere in the room.

Not Maya's.

Not Daniel's.

An old mobile phone sat on the desk, its screen glowing in the darkness.

Maya approached it.

A message appeared.

Day One is almost over.

Then the phone rang again.

Daniel reached for it.

“Don't answer that,” he said.

Maya picked it up.

“Who is this?”

For several seconds, there was only static.

Then a woman's voice whispered, “Maya?”

Maya stopped breathing.

She knew that voice.

She had heard it in childhood memories, in old recordings, and in dreams that left her crying when she woke.

“Mum?”

A quiet sob came through the speaker.

“My baby.”

Maya pressed the phone against her ear.

“Where are you? Are you alive? What happened to you?”

“Listen carefully. You must leave that building immediately.”

“Why?”

“Because he knows you've found the photographs.”

“Who?”

The woman began crying harder.

“The man who killed your father.”

Maya looked at Daniel.

He was staring at her with an expression she couldn't understand.

Her mother continued.

“He will come for you tonight. Don't trust the police. Don't trust your editor. And whatever happens, do not let him take you to Meridian House.”

“Mum, please—”

The line crackled.

A man's voice replaced hers.

“Hello, Maya.”

She recognized it immediately.

The man who had called at midnight.

The man who had predicted the shooting.

The man who knew about her mother.

“Who are you?” she demanded.

“You've spent your entire life searching for answers.”

“Tell me your name!”

A soft laugh came through the speaker.

“You already know me.”

Maya's eyes moved toward the photographs on the wall.

One picture showed a group of doctors standing outside Meridian House. She had studied it earlier that morning.

Now she noticed the man at the far right.

He was younger in the photograph, but his face was unmistakable.

Daniel.

Maya slowly turned toward her editor.

He was standing beside the door, his expression empty.

“Daniel?”

He reached into his jacket.

Maya stepped backward.

“Tell me that's not you.”

Daniel's eyes filled with tears.

“I'm sorry.”

The lights went out.

A crash sounded in the corridor.

Maya heard Daniel shout her name, then the unmistakable sound of a struggle.

She ran toward the door.

Someone grabbed her arm.

She screamed and struck the person with her elbow.

A hand released her.

“Go!” Daniel shouted.

Maya stumbled into the corridor and raced down the stairs.

Behind her, a gunshot echoed through the building.

She didn't stop.

She burst through the side entrance and ran into the street, where she flagged down a passing taxi. She gave the driver an address far from the office building and kept looking behind her until the car disappeared into traffic.

At home, she locked every door and drew every curtain.

Her phone showed 11:58 p.m.

She had less than three minutes before the first day ended.

Maya opened her laptop and created a new folder.

She saved the photographs, the video footage, and every message she had received.

Then she wrote a document titled:

IF I DIE, PUBLISH EVERYTHING.

She attached the files to an email addressed to three trusted journalists and scheduled it to send automatically the following morning.

At 11:59 p.m., her phone vibrated.

A new message.

You were not supposed to survive today.

Maya typed a reply.

Why are you doing this?

The response arrived instantly.

Because you asked the wrong question.

She stared at the screen.

Then another message appeared.

Your mother didn't disappear, Maya.

A third message followed.

She was protecting you.

Maya felt tears gather in her eyes.

For eleven years, she had believed she had been abandoned.

For eleven years, she had blamed herself for the last argument she had with her mother.

She typed with trembling fingers.

Protecting me from what?

The clock changed.

12:01 a.m.

Day Two had begun.

Her phone rang.

Maya answered.

A man's voice whispered, “Tomorrow, at 6:30 p.m., someone you love will die.”

She swallowed.

“Who?”

The man paused.

Then he said, “The person standing outside your door.”

Maya stopped breathing.

A shadow passed beneath the front door.

Someone knocked three times.

She approached slowly and looked through the peephole.

A woman stood in the hallway.

Long dark hair.

Pale-blue dress.

Silver pendant.

Maya's knees nearly buckled.

It was her mother.

Alive.

Standing outside her apartment.

Evelyn raised her head and looked directly into the peephole, as if she knew exactly where Maya was standing.

Then she mouthed five words.

Don't open the door, Maya.

A second figure appeared behind her.

A tall man wearing a grey suit.

He placed one hand on Evelyn's shoulder.

She began to cry.

The man looked directly at the door.

Then he smiled.

Maya stumbled backward as her phone vibrated one final time.

Six days left.
